why.title: Hormuz puts a fuel bill on every air parcel
why.what: Brent has been above $100 since the war began in February.
why.why: Integrators and Asia–Europe air freight pass it on through fuel surcharges.
why.means: Cross-border margins are squeezed just before peak season.

why.title: The $800 free pass is gone. US clearance now runs on data
why.what: The de minimis exemption has been suspended indefinitely since 24 June 2026.
why.why: Duties are now paid monthly by a designated filer, usually the operator.
why.means: An edge for those who master customs data: classification, origin, value.

why.title: A trade truce, but no return to direct small parcels
why.what: Tariff cuts on about $30bn of goods each way in September.
why.why: The US de minimis exemption is not restored by the truce.
why.means: Platforms keep moving stock into local warehouses.

newsletter.subject: WhyItLands · Week 41: the small-parcel door closes, and who pays
newsletter.preview: Outside Brazil, every small parcel now needs a solvent importer and clean data. Plus Hormuz, the EU €2 fee and what is coming in October.
minute: The US suspended its $800 de minimis exemption for all modes and repeals it by statute on 1 July 2027.
The EU charges €3 per tariff line on parcels under €150 since July; a €2 handling fee per item follows on 1 November.
Hormuz: no ceasefire, the strait runs on Iranian permits and Brent was $104 on 28 September.

number.label: Brent per barrel at midday on 28 September, up from $67.33 a year earlier. It reaches the parcel through jet fuel and integrator surcharges.
